key_points: An unsigned editorial reprints the founding June 1952 "The Open Society" editorial marking the journal's 51st year, reframing India's fight against totalitarianism and communism as today's fight against religious fundamentalism and communalism.

A "Going By Instinct" editorial on 9/11, Godhra, and the looming Iraq war argues the "war on terrorism" rhetoric enabled both India's POTA law and the Gujarat pogrom, while taking the position that Iraq bears responsibility for defying UN disarmament resolutions.

Nagindas Sanghavi opens the "Only Politicians, No Statesmen" symposium by arguing the BJP's December 2002 Gujarat win (127 seats, 51% vote) was a continuation of a trend visible since 1995 rather than a post-Godhra landslide, faulting the Congress's outsourced campaign under Kamalnath and the media's failed pre-poll predictions.

Ashok Karnik's "A Wake Up Call From Gujarat" argues the result was a defeat of how secularism was practiced, not of the principle itself, criticising the Congress's "soft Hindutva" temple-visit campaigning and unsubstantiated post-Godhra conspiracy theories blaming the VHP.

A. D. Moddie poses nine pointed questions to Hindutva ideologues, contrasting "cultural nationalism" with Rajaji's self-control and Amartya Sen's account of a "receptive and creative" Indian culture, and challenging the movement to address corruption and land-grabbing at pilgrimage sites.

Cyrus Guzder's "Bridging the Communal Divide: 1" argues uncompromising constitutional citizenship, applied equally regardless of religion, is now the only workable ideology, citing the Shiv Sena's unpunished arson of a Muslim-owned hospital in Thane.

Satish Sahney's companion piece argues the Hindu-Muslim divide will keep spreading unless both communities' fundamentalism is checked, urging that the word "secular" be retired since it is read as anti-Hindu code, and that reconciliation efforts should focus on youth.

The issue also carries a "With Many Voices" digest of press quotations on Gujarat and communalism, and a tribute by Minoo Shroff to Nani Palkhivala, the constitutional lawyer and Forum of Free Enterprise stalwart who died in December 2002.
Freedom First No. 457 (April-June 2003), edited by S. V. Raju, runs a three-part "Only Politicians No Statesmen" symposium framed through "The Bihar Perspective."

Shanker Prasad Tekriwal's "Laloo's Lathi Raj" catalogues failures in education, welfare and rural electrification under the Laloo-Rabri Devi government, and accuses it of corruption including the fodder and bitumen scams.

Manuwant Choudhary's "Living Dangerously in Bihar" gives a first-person account of the state's decline after the Jharkhand bifurcation, covering CARE-India's exit, endemic kidnapping-for-ransom, and naxal violence, and argues Nitish Kumar is no credible alternative to Laloo.
Manoje Nath's "The Bihari: Prisoner of his Own Image" argues the self-effacing "Bihari" stereotype is a psychological trap that keeps Biharis from demanding their fair share of national resources.

Major General E. D'Souza's "Captains Courageous" profiles Field Marshal Cariappa, General K. S. Thimayya, and Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw as evidence that India has in fact produced genuine military statesmen, rebutting the magazine's own framing question.
The issue carries obituary tributes to P. R. Brahmananda, S. Ramakrishnan, and K. F. Rustamji, alongside a report marking the V. B. Karnik birth centenary.

Arvind Deshpande contributes a short piece giving a liberal view on the Iraq War, and Prem Vaidya opens a longer feature on General Sir Arthur "Maharishi" Cotton, the East India Company engineer credited as father of Indian irrigation in the Godavari and Cauvery deltas.

Freedom First No. 459 (Oct-Dec 2003) is dedicated to Satyendra Kumar Dubey, the NHAI engineer murdered in Gaya, Bihar after exposing corruption on the Golden Quadrilateral project; an unsigned piece details the bureaucratic mishandling of his complaint and calls for "hundreds of Satyendra Dubeys."
The issue concludes the year-long "What India Needs" cover series, drawn from a September 2003 seminar at St. Xavier's College, Mumbai.

A. D. Moddie's keynote argues India inherited and perpetuated a colonial administrative architecture, citing a Fraser Institute/Centre for Civil Society study ranking India 86th of 123 countries on economic freedom, and calls for a coalition to build countervailing power against an unaccountable political class.

Jiban K. Mukhopadhyay makes the economic case for a feasible 7% growth rate led by agriculture, citing China's post-1978 reform sequencing, and argues full engagement with WTO negotiations gives India more leverage than the IMF or World Bank.

Nagindas Sanghavi diagnoses corruption, criminalisation and communalism as intertwined diseases, citing India's shortage of judges relative to Western democracies, and admits he has no solution to offer for communalism.

Sadanand Varde argues social justice requires equalising real opportunity, not just formal legal equality, recounting caste-based violence in rural Maharashtra and proposing a constitutional "right to recall" non-performing elected representatives.
The Indian Liberal Group's election appeal opening the issue calls for clean candidates, transparency, and continued economic liberalisation tempered by equity.

Freedom First No. 460 (Jan-Mar 2004) marks the birth centenary of freedom fighter Yusuf Meherally with two tribute essays, while the editorial notes the issue was delayed and cut to 44 pages for lack of advertising.

S. V. Raju's "Of Cabbages & Kings" recounts a Delhi workshop to draft "A Liberal Strategy for India: 2004 and Beyond" that collapsed into factional manoeuvring, closing by invoking Masani's and Rajagopalachari's insistence that a liberal party pursue principle rather than chase power.

Kisan Mehta's reminiscence recalls Yusuf Meherally's tenderness toward fellow prisoners at Yeravada jail, their secret correspondence under aliases, and Meherally's late-life work organising a freedom-struggle exhibition from his sickbed.

G. S. Bhargava's tribute narrates Meherally's life from his 1928 leadership of the "Simon Go Back" protests through his break with his guardian M. A. Jinnah, his Congress Socialist Party co-founding, and his death in 1950 at 47 from a lathi injury sustained years earlier.

A. D. Moddie's "India's First 21st Century General Elections" surveys the eve of the 2004 poll, describing a "600 million schizophrenic" electorate and assessing a maturing BJP/NDA, a dynastically-trapped Congress, and a Left overtaken by history.
Manuwant Choudhary's open letter reproaches Sharad Joshi for allying the Shetkari Sanghatana with the NDA, invoking Minoo Masani's vision of a "Swatantra Bharat Party" as a betrayed liberal dream.

Former Prime Minister Chandrashekhar, interviewed by R. Rajagopalan, criticises opportunistic shifts among India's political leadership and calls for cross-party unity on shared national-interest questions such as agriculture.
Amitabh's short story "Pad (Carrion)," introduced as a depiction of pre-Ambedkar Mahar community life, opens with a shanty town's frantic, unresolved scramble to butcher a dead cow found at dawn.
Freedom First No. 461 (April-June 2004) opens with an obituary tribute to Justice V. M. Tarkunde, extracted from an address by Attorney General Soli Sorabjee.
The cover feature reports a May 2004 Mumbai discussion on "India's Festival of Democracy - Elections 2004," organised with the Indian Liberal Group and the Project for Economic Education.

S. V. Raju warns the Election Commission's autonomy is at risk from government dependence for manpower and funds, citing the 720-fold rise in election costs since 1967 and instances of the EC straying beyond its mandate.

Nagindas Sanghavi argues the 2004 campaign again failed to surface substantive issues, framing the BJP's retreat from militant Hindutva toward "India Shining" and the Congress's revival as personal validation of Sonia Gandhi's dynastic leadership.

Ashok Karnik argues the narrow BJP-Congress seat gap reflected no decisive ideological verdict, warning that anti-incumbency and demand for "instant delivery" risk pushing governments toward short-termist populism.

Uttara Sahasrabuddhe contends only six states effectively determine national power, reframing India's run of hung parliaments as a reflection of social diversity rather than instability, and identifies an emerging bipolar Congress-BJP polity.
Floor discussion at the meeting covered disputes over criminal-record disclosure for candidates, electoral-roll disenfranchisement, and the politicisation of Sonia Gandhi's foreign origin.
Freedom First No. 462 (July-Sept 2004) is dedicated to Abe Solomon, the magazine's longtime patron and fundraiser, alongside an obituary for Radical Humanist Dr. Indumati Parikh.

The cover feature, "The Liberal Budget - Building an Equitable Society," presented by S. V. Raju as a joint Indian Liberal Group/Project for Economic Education effort, offers the first liberal alternative to the government's annual Union Budget.

Raju's essay grounds the Liberal Budget in Ludwig von Mises's distinction between liberalism and socialism as a matter of means not ends, setting nine numeric human-development targets for 2007 and 2012 and calling for abolishing discretionary tax search-and-seizure powers.

The Liberal Budget summary argues disinvestment should be tested by whether the state belongs in an activity at all, calls for lifting agricultural land ceilings and internal trade barriers, and for genuinely independent regulators.

Major General E. D'Souza's "Indian Troops in World War II" argues the contribution of Indian soldiers, who won 37 Victoria Crosses, has been erased from British and American memory, crediting Baroness Sheila Flather's campaign for the Hyde Park Corner Memorial Gate.

Prem Vaidya reviews the Eighth Mumbai International Film Festival, including a tribute to Leni Riefenstahl and documentaries on youth suicide in Kerala, a 1971 war rape survivor in Bangladesh, and forced tribal-marriage settlements in Pakistan.

Louella Lobo Prabhu's satirical column comments on M. F. Hussain's controversial career, a Supreme Court ruling that the right to strike is not fundamental, and the forcible shutdown of screenings of the film "Girl Friend" over its lesbian subject matter.
"Of Cabbages and Kings" welcomes Manmohan Singh's appointment as Prime Minister while criticising the politicisation of Governors' appointments under successive governments.

Freedom First No. 463 (Oct-Dec 2004) is built around a birth-centenary tribute to founder Minoo Masani, reprinting his essays "Leadership" and "I Believe" alongside S. V. Raju's retrospective "Minoo Masani - The Principled Politician."

Raju traces Masani's journey from founding the Congress Socialist Party in 1934 through his break with its Moscow-directed wing, his 1944 "Socialism Reconsidered," and his 1959 co-founding of the Swatantra Party with C. Rajagopalachari.

In "Leadership," Masani argues India suffers a shortage of genuine leadership due to cultural deference and political "tailism," contrasting Churchill and de Gaulle's conditional leadership with Indian equivocation and quoting Walter Lippmann's warning about authoritarian temptation.
In "I Believe," Masani professes a humanist Brotherhood of Man ethic grounded in Stoic philosophy, tracing how contact with Gandhi's linkage of ends and means led him to renounce State Socialism.

"Of Cabbages and Kings" comments on sycophantic press coverage of Indira Gandhi, calls Yasser Arafat "the father of modern terrorism" on his death, and warns of Bush's re-election implications for civil liberties.

R. M. Lala's "Three Great Liberals" profiles Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, and Jamsetji Tata as London-shaped founders of Indian liberalism, crediting Naoroji as the first Indian elected to the British Parliament.
V. Balachandran explains U.S. Electoral College mechanics to rebut Indian media claims that the Supreme Court "elected" Bush in 2000, drawing a parallel to the 1961 Hawaii electors dispute.
The editor's note announces the postponement of the Indian Liberal Group's Second National Convention to February 2005 and notes the death of Times columnist Bernard Levin.

Freedom First No. 464 (Jan-Mar 2005) is a Convention Special issue for the Indian Liberal Group's Second National Convention in Mangalore, opening with an excerpt from Minoo Masani's autobiography "Against the Tide" recounting the Indian Liberal Group's 1965 founding.

Masani describes distributing the Swatantra Party's 21 principles to the Liberal International's Executive Committee at Gardone in 1959, and names Sophia Wadia, Khushwant Singh, B. R. Shenoy, and H. V. R. Iengar among the ILG's founding executive committee.

A. D. Moddie argues coalition management and accountable governance will define India's 21st century, using Bihar's decline and rising unorganised-sector unemployment as case studies, and proposes renaming the Ministry of Labour a Ministry for National Employment and Productivity.

Moddie proposes multi-party youth committees, naming figures like Rahul Gandhi, Jyotiraditya Scindia, and Milind Deora, to tackle population planning, panchayati raj reform, and employability training.

S. P. Sathe treats accountability as a moral concept, tracing the Supreme Court's closure of a chief-minister reappointment loophole, its mandated candidate disclosure of assets and criminal records, and the growing institutional legitimacy of the Election Commission under T. N. Seshan.

Sathe cites Public Interest Litigation, liberalised after the Emergency, as a key civil-society accountability tool exposing ordinance abuse and corrupt cement-allotment practices, and credits the National Human Rights Commission's intervention in Gujarat carnage cases.

Ajit Karnik surveys India's post-1991 economic liberalisation, crediting it with a fall in poverty from 37% to about 26% while warning of worsening state government finances, and invokes Hayek's "Fatal Conceit" to critique the planning-era state.

Freedom First No. 465 (April-June 2005) devotes its cover feature, "From Tibet to TAR," to five essays marking the 46th anniversary of the Tibetan National Uprising Day and the Dalai Lama's March 10, 2005 statement.

Ajay B. Agrawal's "The Annexation of Tibet — India's Shameful Role" argues Tibet was fully independent until 1950, and that Nehru's government conceded a "vague suzerainty of China" it could not later escape, quoting Sardar Patel's prescient 1950 warning letter.

Claude Arpi's "The Irony of the Bandung Conference" argues the 1955 Bandung Conference's anti-colonial rhetoric masked Tibet's abandonment, citing Acharya Kripalani's description of the Panchsheel Agreement as "born in sin."

The Dalai Lama's own March 10, 2005 statement reaffirms the Middle Way Approach seeking genuine autonomy rather than independence, while acknowledging Chinese economic development in Tibet alongside continued human-rights concerns.

Aspi Mistry rebuts press coverage claiming the Dalai Lama "gave up" the demand for a free Tibet, and Pema Thinley's reprinted Tibetan Review editorial argues global commercial self-interest, from the EU's arms-embargo debate to US retreat from UN pressure, leaves China facing no real accountability.

Tenzin Tsundue, writing as a second-generation exile, describes the 20,000-member Tibetan Youth Congress's generational impatience with the "Genuine Autonomy" compromise and its demand for full independence.

A reprint of Minoo Masani's 1956 essay "Why I Oppose Communism," marking his birth centenary, traces his journey from socialist sympathies to anti-Communism grounded in Lord Acton's axiom that liberty is the supreme good.

"Of Cabbages and Kings" comments on India's UN Security Council ambitions, a Supreme Court ruling permitting caste-exclusive housing societies, and criticises the Maharashtra government's dance-bar ban as moral posturing.

Freedom First No. 466 (July-Sept 2005) was delayed after Mumbai's unprecedented flooding destroyed the editor's papers and computer, forcing abandonment of a planned cover feature on India-Pakistan rapprochement.

S. V. Raju's tribute to C. R. Irani, the late Statesman editor, credits him with preserving the paper's independence during the Emergency and recounts his history in the Swatantra Party at Minoo Masani's invitation.

A reprint marking Minoo Masani's birth centenary, his 1957 Minute of Dissent on the Wealth Tax Bill, argues extending the tax to joint-stock companies would harm small investors, citing Reserve Bank survey data showing most Bombay shareholders were middle- or lower-income.

Major General Eustace D'Souza surveys China's expanding military modernisation, including a "Web Army" monitoring Indian missions and the militarisation of Tibet via the Gormu-Lhasa railway, and recommends India strengthen border forces and regional diplomacy.

A press release by Aspi B. Mistry describes Chinese diplomatic pressure to cancel a Mumbai talk by the Dalai Lama's translator, recalling a similar 2004 episode that forced a Tibet retrospective out of the Asian Film Festival.

Dr. R. Srinivasan profiles 19th-century rationalist Gopal Ganesh Agarkar as the most sceptical of Indian liberals on religion's role in public life, reviewing Aravind Ganachari's biography on the centenary of Agarkar's death.
Ashok Karnik examines the controversy over L. K. Advani's praise for Jinnah's 1947 speech, surveying competing theories for the remark and the resulting RSS-BJP disarray.
Tributes by Humera Ahmed and Laeeq Futehally remember novelist Shama Futehally, situating her fiction's sensitivity to privileged women confronting a harsher world.

Freedom First No. 467 (Oct-Dec 2005) leads on rising intolerance in Indian public life, centred on Soli Sorabjee's Minoo Masani Birth Centenary Lecture arguing that a free press and independent judiciary are democracy's two indispensable prerequisites.

Sorabjee catalogues Indian and global episodes of censorship and mob intimidation, including the Bhandarkar Institute vandalism over James Laine's Shivaji biography and the Supreme Court's Jehovah's Witnesses ruling protecting students who stayed silent during the anthem.

Geeta Doctor's companion piece reads Tamil Nadu's "L'Affaire Kushboo" controversy, alongside a university dress code and the arrest of two hotel employees over a party photo, as intolerance weaponised against women and modern lifestyles.

V. Balachandran summarises a paper arguing terrorism should be treated as a crime rather than a political grievance, detailing the human and financial toll of Pakistan-sponsored terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir.
R. Srinivasan traces the publishing history of Gandhi's banned Hind Swaraj in Madras, noting the city uniquely had three simultaneous publishers of the work.
Shukla Bose of the Parikrma Humanity Foundation opens an essay arguing corporate social responsibility must move beyond philanthropic add-ons to genuine, CEO-led institutional commitment.
An obituary tribute by Vilas B. Patankar remembers D. B. Karnik, a humanist journalist devoted to M. N. Roy's radical humanist movement.

Freedom First No. 468 (Jan-Mar 2006) devotes its cover feature, "Prospects for the Party System in India," to a symposium on coalition politics after the fragmentation of Congress's one-party dominance.

Amit Dholakia traces India's shift from the "Congress system" to today's fragmented, arithmetic-driven coalitions, warning of an "end of ideology" and calling for legislation on party funding and candidate vetting.

A. Vaidyanathan's Ambirajan Memorial Lecture credits India's constitutional design and watchdog institutions with a resilient democracy, while arguing the political class has hollowed out institutional independence through manipulated appointments.

Sharad Bailur, revisiting a 1998 Freedom First argument, insists coalitions are an aberration of splintering ambition rather than voter sophistication, and proposes a two-round electoral runoff system while defending universal suffrage against Nani Palkhivala's proposed literacy restriction.

V. N. Torgal argues the BJP's post-Ayodhya rise, not deliberate design, produced today's bipolar contest, and warns this drift could devour liberal and secular forces in a diverse country better served by decentralisation.
S. V. Raju reports on Minoo Masani Birth Centenary commemorations held across several Indian cities.
The late Professor S. P. Sathe's posthumously published essay examines Parliament versus the Supreme Court over the expulsion of MPs in a cash-for-questions scandal.

Freedom First No. 469 (April-June 2006) devotes its cover feature, "The Makeover from Ideology to National Self-Interest," to India's foreign-policy shift from Nehruvian non-alignment toward realist, US-friendly diplomacy, centred on the pending Indo-US civil nuclear deal.

B. Ramesh Babu traces the paradigm shift from Indira Gandhi's post-Emergency de-control policy through the 1991 crisis to the BJP-led NDA's courtship of Washington after Pokhran-II, while warning India has lost moral standing as a spokesman for the developing world.

Sharad Bailur, via a Cold War counterfactual, argues economic strength rather than military power decided global bipolarity's end, and warns the US pursues a "two-track" policy capping India's nuclear capacity while cultivating friendliness.

Maj. Gen. Eustace D'Souza frames the nuclear deal as a choice between a constraining "trick" and a beneficial "treat," arguing the NPT's structure inherently discriminates against India and urging India accept fuel supply while resisting any security-compromising conditions.

Firoze Hirjikaka's polemic asks whether India is a genuine democracy, applying Lincoln's Gettysburg definition to argue Indian legislators are unrepresentative and voters complicit through venality and apathy.

A. Vaidyanathan's concluding Ambirajan Memorial Lecture instalment credits democratic competition with forcing anti-poverty spending for scheduled castes and tribes, while criticising proliferating, unverified, centrally imposed schemes that leave panchayats with no real accountability role.

Freedom First No. 470 (July 2006) devotes its cover feature to a return engagement with reservations, reporting on a June 2006 Mumbai seminar convened after Union Minister Arjun Singh proposed extending OBC reservation by 27% in central higher-education institutions.

Dr. Usha Thakkar argues identity politics has displaced the constitutional vision of reservation as a time-bound "enabling provision," surveying wildly conflicting OBC population estimates from the Mandal Commission, NSS, and CSDS.

Brig. S. C. Sharma traces reservation's history from princely-state origins through the Kalelkar and Mandal Commissions to the 2005 constitutional amendment extending quotas to private institutions, comparing India's experience to the modest community-level gains of US civil-rights-era affirmative action.

J. B. D'Souza argues "merit" prized by elite exams is itself manufactured by expensive schooling, pointing to Bihar's "Super 30" coaching programme as the grassroots intervention Mandal recommended but which was ignored.

Sharad Bailur frames the debate through Rawls's Theory of Justice, arguing private-sector reservation is unworkable because firms answer to shareholders, and tells the story of a Dalit classmate who chose the open category over reservation to become Chief Secretary.
R. K. Hebsur's opening pages argue a "double game" is underway around OBC classification, with dominant landed non-Savarna castes lobbying for inclusion to capture benefits.
Freedom First No. 471 (August 2006), marking the journal's return to monthly publication after 21 years, is dominated by the aftermath of the July 11, 2006 Mumbai train bombings.

Ashok Karnik's lead essay traces the transnational ideology of "Islamic Jehad" from Hassan al-Turabi's doctrine through a chronology of attacks culminating in the Mumbai blasts, recommending better intelligence and anti-terror-financing reforms.

Sharad Bailur argues India's constitutional commitment to liberty has produced a "soft state" vulnerable to terrorism, proposing Israeli-style measures including mandatory unappealable death sentences and a dedicated anti-terrorist finance department.
R. Srinivasan marks the bicentenary of the 1806 Vellore Mutiny, questioning whether it and 1857 constitute genuine proto-nationalist uprisings or a retrospectively constructed myth.

Three contributors continue the reservations symposium: Bapu Satyanarayana criticises Arjun Singh's 27% OBC quota as political self-preservation, Saratchandra Panda argues rural employment creation matters more than reservation, and Santosh Nedungadi argues reservation has served its purpose and should be phased out over a decade.

V. Balachandran profiles Cold War diplomat George Kennan, correcting an Indian newspaper's misdated obituary and describing Kennan's regret over the militarised distortion of his "containment" doctrine.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" column addresses the rape and murder of a child domestic servant by an upper-middle-class Mumbai family, arguing Indian employers treat domestic help with dehumanising entitlement.

Freedom First No. 472 (September 2006) opens with Sharad Bailur's critique of the proposed Indian Post Office Amendment Bill, arguing the Department of Posts should adapt to new technology rather than expand its delivery monopoly and tax courier operators.
Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" stages opposing views on six live controversies, from electronic-media censorship to the Volcker-report allegations against Natwar Singh.

Sharad Joshi indicts Prime Minister Manmohan Singh's Vidarbha relief package as inadequate against farmer indebtedness, blaming the Maharashtra Cotton Monopoly Procurement Scheme for an estimated Rs. 30,000 crore loss to Vidarbha farmers and calling for a separate Vidarbha state.

V. N. Torgal revisits the 1932 Gandhi-Ambedkar disagreement over separate electorates to argue OBCs still need reservation, while questioning whether Ambedkar's "creamy layer" filtration theory has actually worked.

Wipro chairman Azim H. Premji argues Indian children, whether in zari factories or elite exam-driven schools, are equally stripped of the freedom of childhood, invoking Gandhi's view that adults learn from children.

C. A. Kallianpur explains the historical basis of the Tibet dispute, arguing Tibet's protectorate relationship was with Manchu China specifically, not the Han-majority state that emerged from the 1911-12 revolution.
R. Srinivasan memorialises Naguib Mahfouz and Pramoedya Ananta Toer, two literary figures who died weeks apart in 2006, both having suffered persecution for their writing.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" questions profiling logic after Indian passengers were detained in Amsterdam, and separately welcomes the Soli Sorabjee police-reform committee's proposals while doubting Parliament will pass them intact.

Freedom First No. 473 (October 2006) explains a new bi-tier publication schedule -- 12-page monthly issues and 48-page quarterlies -- and devotes its cover feature to the widening gap between India's booming economy and its declining quality of governance.

An obituary recalls Dalit leader Kanshi Ram, founder of the Bahujan Samaj Party, as an amoral but historically significant political strategist who made OBCs and Dalits a numerical force through his protegee Mayawati.
S. L. N. Simha's "Dharma in Politics" argues declining ethical standards trace to the erosion of Dharma, citing a World Bank governance-indicators report ranking India poorly among 213 countries.

R. Srinivasan's "Things Fall Apart; the Centre Cannot Hold" cites Karnataka Chief Minister Kumaraswamy's family acquiring a Rs. 36-crore IT park within 51 days of taking office, contrasting today's venality with the trusteeship ethic of Y. B. Chavan, Kamaraj, and Jayaprakash Narayan.
Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" weighs the Malegaon blasts, disqualification of tainted politicians, the Indo-US nuclear treaty, and the India-Pakistan Havana declaration from opposing angles.

Sharad Joshi's Rajya Sabha speech, "The Tragedy of Being a Farmer in India," traces farmer suicides to the Green Revolution's failure to secure remunerative prices, estimating negative price support cost farmers roughly Rs. 300,000 crores between 1980 and 2000.

"Of Cabbages and Kings" reports the Supreme Court's 2006 order finally allowing uncut telecast of Anand Patwardhan's documentary "Father, Son and Holy War," and criticises Karnataka's Belgaum politicking over Tipu Sultan's place in textbooks.

Freedom First No. 474 (November 2006) leads on the diplomatic theatre around Chinese President Hu Jintao's state visit, covering the government's attempts to keep the Dalai Lama and Tibetan groups quiet.

The lead story recounts Tenzin Tsundue's 14-day house arrest in Dharamsala and Lhakpa Tsering's self-immolation attempt outside Bombay's Taj Hotel, timed to Hu Jintao's summit speech, alongside a joint Tibetan-organisation memorandum urging India not to compromise on Tibet in border talks.
Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" debates General Musharraf's memoir, the Mohd. Afzal Guru death-sentence controversy, and whether an assertive judiciary is overstepping into executive territory.
A reprint of U.S. District Judge William Young's sentencing statement to shoe-bomber Richard Reid is presented as demonstrating the correct legal distinction between soldiers and terrorists.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" column, prompted by a cancelled Berlin opera depicting severed religious heads, questions how far freedom of expression should extend when weighed against the risk of violent backlash.
Feroza Seervai argues against caste-based reservation in higher education, contending that unequal schooling, not innate ability, explains gaps in academic preparedness.
Subroto Roy's tribute to Milton Friedman, who died that month, recounts Friedman's suppressed 1955 memorandum advising India's Second Five Year Plan and his mentorship of Roy over two decades.
Freedom First No. 476 (January 2007) leads with the cover story "Crime and Punishment," opening with a tribute to constitutional jurist H. M. Seervai on his birth centenary.

Ashok Karnik's cover essay surveys crime and punishment in India, crediting the RTI Act and reversed verdicts in the Mattoo and Lall cases as hopeful signs while indicting the police as the most feared yet least trusted institution and citing a conviction rate of only 6.5%.

R. Srinivasan and Seetha's companion essays frame the Nithari child-killings as evidence that "the Right to Life has become a casualty," with Seetha identifying affluent Noida employers as a "collective culprit" for ignoring the missing children's disappearance.

Singapore diplomat Kishore Mahbubani's reproduced speech predicts India will increasingly claim credit for democratic traditions while rediscovering indigenous political thought and resuming its historic role as a civilisational meeting point.

Ganesh Sovani's essay on political corruption cites India's worsening Transparency International ranking and notes that no Indian politician has ever been jailed on corruption charges, due to Section 19 immunity in the Prevention of Corruption Act.

Subroto Roy argues neither the Congress-Left establishment nor the BJP-RSS opposition offers a genuine classical-liberal alternative, concluding India still lacks a non-geriatric, non-sycophantic liberal party.

P. R. Dubhashi's "Rural Perspective" argues farmer suicides across five states reflect deep structural agrarian distress, criticising the finance minister for prioritising stock indices over rural distress.

Freedom First No. 477 (February 2007) leads with Sunil S. Bhandare's essay arguing the state should exit business and manufacturing, recommending the government target at least Rs. 25,000 crores from disinvestment in the 2007-08 budget.
G. G. Parikh's tribute remembers socialist leader Professor Sadanand Varde, who held public office without personal benefit and championed the right to die with dignity.

Anderson Cooper's introduction to the Committee to Protect Journalists' 2006 report records 55 journalists killed worldwide for their work, 32 in Iraq, and recounts the murder of Russian journalist Anna Politkovskaya.
Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" debates Pranab Mukherjee's Pakistan visit and the racist treatment of Shilpa Shetty on British reality television.
S. Jagadisan's essay on Nehru as a "literary gaol bird" traces the composition of his prison-written works, including "Glimpses of World History" and "The Discovery of India."

R. Srinivasan profiles Nobel laureate Orhan Pamuk's prosecution under Turkish law for discussing the Armenian and Kurdish killings, closing on the assassination of fellow journalist Hrant Dink days before Pamuk's Nobel award.
Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" questions the puritanical standard applied to American political leaders' private morality, contrasting it with French attitudes toward Segolene Royal.
Freedom First No. 478 (March 2007) features a discussion on discipline and morale in the Indian Army, and a second essay on agricultural futures trading.

Brig. S. C. Sharma surveys procurement scandals, Kargil-era grievances, and rising court appeals over postings, arguing these reflect India's litigious culture rather than genuine indiscipline, and faults Nehru-era governments for never implementing an Army Council-style grievance mechanism.

Sharma defines morale as decisive but unmeasurable, citing political interference, poor pay, and confused counter-insurgency signalling as threats, and calls for compulsory military service if volunteer numbers keep falling.

Sharad Joshi's "Why Futures are Farmer Friendly" argues the government's ban on wheat and paddy futures trading, announced the day after farmers' groups planned to sell through a futures exchange, was a populist move that cornered farmers into low Food Corporation of India procurement prices.
Joshi cites government inflation data showing non-futures-traded food items rose comparably or more than futures-traded ones, arguing this refutes the claim that futures trading drives price rises.
Freedom First No. 479 (April 2007) devotes its cover package, "Return of the Permit-Licence Raj," to the UPA government's Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Bill, 2006, debated from three angles.

Ganesh Sovani cautiously defends the need for regulation given security concerns, citing the 2006 Mumbai train blasts and a CBI finding against the Abdul Kalam Azad Islamic Awakening Centre for concealing foreign donations.

Ashok Karnik, a former Deputy Director of the Intelligence Bureau, frames the Bill as a "protection or persecution" dilemma, proposing a compromise threshold exempting NGOs receiving less than a set annual sum.

The Voluntary Action Network India's unsigned critique calls the Bill "draconian," warning its 50% cap on administrative expenses and subjective "political nature" test would especially harm small research NGOs.
P. M. Kamath criticises the government's practice of delaying visas for Fulbright scholars as an outdated Cold War reflex, given more than 7,500 scholars have used the exchange programme since 1950.

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" debates the reopened Bofors case following Quattrocchi's arrest, the Supreme Court's stay on OBC reservations, and Rahul Gandhi's Deoband remarks disowning responsibility for the Babri Masjid demolition.

Freedom First No. 480 (May 2007) leads with Sharad Joshi's essay on global warming's threat to Indian agriculture, citing Delhi's peak temperature reportedly rising from 30°C in 2005 to 38.3°C in 2007.

Joshi criticises the Supreme Court's stay on GMO trials for blocking Indian-developed drought- and salinity-resistant crops, and warns crossbred dairy cattle and food processing face mounting climate strain.

Nitin Pai argues India's energy security lies in domestic port and pipeline infrastructure rather than the Iran-Pakistan-India gas pipeline, which would route gas through Baloch-contested territory and hand Pakistan a bargaining chip.

Shibayan Raha recounts the 1995 disappearance of the 11th Panchen Lama, Gendhun Choekyi Nyima, three days after the Dalai Lama's recognition, and renews calls for his release now that he has turned 18.
An unsigned report tracks stalled compliance with the Supreme Court's Prakash Singh police-reform directives, finding only 11% of states fully compliant.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" condemns the lenient sentence in the Alistair Pereira hit-and-run case and political interference shielding a university vandal, while Kusum Choppra critiques the corporatisation of Indian healthcare at rural healthcare's expense.
The editor's note frames Mayawati's 2007 Uttar Pradesh victory as a potential shift away from decades of caste- and religion-based political mobilisation.

Freedom First No. 481 (June 2007) leads with a report on an ICCF-sponsored discussion on artistic freedom, prompted by the Baroda University vandalism incident and the M. F. Hussain painting controversy.

R. Srinivasan's report surveys the debate between Justice Holmes's "clear and present danger" free-speech standard and calls for artistic freedom to be bounded by religious sensitivity, noting the asymmetry in how majority and minority religious sensitivities are treated.

Bharat Jhunjhunwala and Ganesh Sovani argue the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 2002 would entrench a loss-making Department of Posts monopoly and invite corruption, proposing courier taxation instead of restriction.

Sharad Joshi criticises a proposal for a new price-fixing board with compulsory agricultural procurement, arguing for scrapping the Essential Commodities Act's restrictions instead so farmers can capture market prices.

Shashi Shekhar traces the Constitution's Ninth Schedule from Nehru's 1951 First Amendment to the Supreme Court's January 2007 ruling opening post-1973 Schedule laws to judicial review, arguing India still lacks a genuine right-of-centre constituency committed to individual freedom.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" catalogues a string of 2007 religious-vigilantism incidents, warning that public silence toward fundamentalist violence mirrors the conditions that enabled Nazi persecution in Germany.

An obituary for Professor S. V. Kogekar accompanies his final book review of Prem Shankar Jha's "The Twilight of the Nation State," which he praises for its critique of US unilateralism while faulting its romanticised view of national sovereignty.

Freedom First No. 482 (July 2007) devotes its cover feature, "Chinese Chakkar," to seven essays on India-China relations, rejecting naive "Hindi-Chini Bhai Bhai" sentiment in favour of a clear-eyed accounting of the relationship.

T. C. A. Rangachari compares India's and China's parallel post-war rise, contrasting China's pragmatic, ideology-free foreign-policy pivots with India's more principle-constrained diplomacy, including its consistent support for China's UN membership after 1962.

P. M. Kamath examines how American commentators, including Selig Harrison and Samuel Huntington, read the US-India civil nuclear deal partly as a hedge against China's rise, noting China is the deal's most vocal opponent.

B. Ramesh Babu argues China remains a strategic rival despite shared developing-world interests, citing "cartographic aggression" and Beijing's use of Pakistan, Nepal, Burma and Bangladesh to contain India.

Claude Arpi's "Engaging China: Historical Perspectives" traces renewed Chinese pressure over the Tawang sector in 2007, including a scholar's public call for India to "return" Tawang and a disputed May 2007 incursion report denied by state and military officials.
"Of Cabbages and Kings" criticises the Congress-led UPA's manipulation of Pratibha Patil's presidential candidacy and the government's weak defence of Dr. Mohamed Haneef, detained in Australia.
Freedom First No. 483 (August 2007), published as India marked its 60th Independence anniversary, frames its stance as "sober reflection, not manufactured media hype."

P. Koshy argues rural cyber enterprises, backed by NGOs like n-Logue and the Byrraju Foundation, can create jobs and realise a pragmatic Gandhian "gram-swaraj" while warning of a coming "creative destruction" phase.

Nitin Pai's "Contained by China" argues China deliberately keeps the border dispute unresolved as a containment tool, recommending India reconstitute the Rajya Sabha along US Senate lines to give border states like Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh equal representation.

Sharad Joshi's "Sanjeevani for Agriculture" profiles farm success stories that occurred despite, not because of, government intervention, including Madhavrao More's champagne-rivalling "Pimpagne" wine venture shut down by licensing rules.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" argues post-Godhra Hindu nationalism has grown assertive enough to rival Islamist intolerance, citing the Bhandarkar Institute vandalism and Shiv Sena's cybercafe attacks over Orkut.
Faiyaz Hardwarewala argues the Prime Minister was wrong to publicly criticise high CEO salaries on grounds of government overreach into private company affairs, not because the salaries are deserved.

Prof. V. C. Phadke reviews Anita Kainthla's biography of Baba Amte, tracing his transformation from a wealthy young man to founder of the Anandwan leprosy settlement and participant in the Narmada Bachao Andolan.

Freedom First No. 484 (September 2007) leads with the Sethusamudram Ship Canal controversy and centres on a three-writer symposium on the India-US civil nuclear deal, offering pro, con, and qualified-pro positions.

S. C. Sharma argues the deal grants India a unique NPT exemption and preserves military reactors from inspection; N. S. Venkataraman counters India has 50 years of low-cost uranium and doesn't need the deal; T. S. Gopi Rethinaraj frames it as ending India's "nuclear apartheid."

Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" debates the Ram Setu agitation, the "Kaoboys of RAW" memoir controversy, coalition politics since 1989, and the Sanjay Dutt and Salman Khan celebrity prosecutions.
An extended tribute remembers civil servant J. B. D'Souza, recalling his tip-off to Minoo Masani during a 1975 Emergency arrest threat and his memoir "No Trumpets and Bugles."

Sharad Joshi's "Hot Air Balloons from the Red Fort" criticises Manmohan Singh's 2007 Independence Day address as a retreat into Nehruvian urban-industrial development thinking, contrasting it with Japan's model of deliberately raised agricultural prices funding industrialisation.

A. V. Karnik reviews B. Raman's memoir "The Kaoboys of R&AW," detailing the agency's claimed mole in General Yahya Khan's office ahead of the 1971 war and its simultaneous, sometimes contradictory foreign-intelligence liaisons.

An item reports the fundamentalist assault by Majlis legislators on a Hyderabad event releasing Telugu translations of Taslima Nasreen's books, with legislator Akbaruddin Owaisi reportedly saying he wanted to kill her "without regrets."

Freedom First No. 485 (October 2007) devotes its cover feature, "The Road Most Traveled And Least Followed," to the Gandhi birth-centenary moment and the Bollywood "Gandhigiri" vogue, assembling essays ranging from reverent to sharply revisionist.

Aloo Dastur defends Gandhi's continuing relevance through Truth and Non-Violence, tracing his introduction of passive resistance from South Africa through the Salt Satyagraha and his standoff with Ambedkar over separate electorates.

Writing as "a humble follower of Babasaheb Dr. Ambedkar," Dr. Amitabh indicts Gandhi's record on caste, recalling his exclusion from touching Tilak's body over caste hierarchy and his 1932 fast that forced Ambedkar to give up separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.

Firoze Hirjikaka gives a warts-and-all reflection calling Gandhi "certainly no saint" yet crediting him with defeating the British Empire without conventional weapons, contrasting his stature with contemporary politicians' venality.
Kusum Choppra takes a skeptical view of the commercialised "Gandhigiri" fad, contrasting it with Nelson Mandela's post-prison reconciliation with apartheid's perpetrators.

V. Balachandran examines whether Gandhian non-violence has any purchase against modern terrorism, tracing Gandhi's 1909 rejection of violence after Madanlal Dhingra's assassination of a British official through the Irish Troubles and the 2006 Ayodhya bombing's peaceful aftermath.

Bharat Verma's "The Danger is Real" opens a security-affairs piece warning of threats to India's territorial integrity from a Naxalite corridor linking Nepal to Andhra Pradesh and Kashmir Valley militancy.

Freedom First No. 486 (November 2007) leads with B. Ramesh Babu's essay on India's realpolitik dealings with Myanmar's junta during the 2007 monk-led protests, reprinting extracts of a 1965 Minoo Masani speech on what a Swatantra government would have done on planning and controls.

Nitin Raut condemns the CPI(M)'s handling of the Nandigram land conflict, accusing armed cadres of suppressing villagers resisting SEZ acquisition with alleged police and administration connivance, and criticising the UPA's silence.
Uppili R.'s "De-regulate to Prosper" uses the film Guru and a 2001 McKinsey report to argue delicensing, as in the automobile sector, drives growth that continued agricultural regulation suppresses.

The Society for the Right to Die with Dignity's newsletter carries R. N. Bhaskar's essay invoking Camus to argue for a right to die with dignity, alongside excerpts from H. D. Shourie's 2005 Supreme Court writ petition seeking a "Living Will."

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" reflects on how Gujarati Hindu political attitudes hardened since Godhra into support for Narendra Modi despite the Tehelka sting's revelations of complicity in the violence.

An excerpted campaign piece from saveourearth.co.uk makes the case for boycotting Chinese-made goods on human-rights, environmental, and product-safety grounds, citing sweatshop labour, organ harvesting, and melamine-tainted goods.
C. A. Kallianpur's undelivered welcome address argues Indian public discourse is selectively silent about Chinese colonialism in Tibet and elsewhere while remaining vocal about Western colonialism.

Freedom First No. 487 (December 2007) is dominated by the Nandigram violence, opening with West Bengal Governor Gopalkrishna Gandhi's November 2007 statement condemning the armed "recapture" of Nandigram villages as a "war zone."

An exchange of open letters between Justice V. R. Krishna Iyer and the Governor, and a report on CPI(M) leaders' furious reaction after the Calcutta High Court ruled the March 14 police firing that killed 14 residents unconstitutional.
T. H. Chowdary likens Nandigram to the 1921 Kronstadt uprising and the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown as instances of communist regimes turning violently on their own supporters.

V. Balachandran opens a planned four-part series on national security, arguing globalisation has eroded state control and citing the 2001 Group of Ministers report's broadened definition encompassing non-traditional threats like epidemics and migration.

Firoze Hirjikaka's "Cornucopia" argues India habitually capitulates to diplomatic pressure, citing its failure to extradite Ajmer blast suspects from Bangladesh and its pressuring of Taslima Nasreen to withdraw passages from her autobiography.
Suman Oak launches a new series on Hindu rites and festivals, opening with Makarsankranti and calling for discarding rituals harmful to human dignity while retaining those that foster goodwill.

N. Vittal reviews Feroza H. Seervai's memoir "Winning Without Corruption," highlighting her practical advice for citizens resisting corrupt officialdom through persistence and the right to information.
Freedom First No. 488 (January 2008) opens its New Year issue reflecting on India's post-Independence "revolutions" and persistent poverty.

S. V. Raju revisits the Swatantra Party's 14-year-old Bombay High Court petition seeking Election Commission registration without swearing allegiance to socialism, quoting Minoo Masani's essay on Liberalism to explain the party's actual relationship to socialism's aims.

Amit Dholakia analyses the BJP's December 2007 Gujarat landslide under Narendra Modi, attributing the win to Modi's personal charisma and administrative record rather than a referendum on Hindutva, while cautioning that Gujarat's human-development indices still lag its growth.

Ashish Puntambekar argues Benazir Bhutto's assassination has made a political solution in Pakistan nearly impossible, warning of possible Sindhi separatism, a jihadi takeover, and a refugee influx of four to five million people into India.
Ashok Karnik's "Point Counter Point" debates the death of democracy in Pakistan, the Modi phenomenon, the Rane-Deshmukh rift in Maharashtra Congress, and the Pawar-Thackeray meeting.

Cyrus Guzder revisits Minoo Masani's 1969 Rajaji Memorial Lecture "Too Much Politics, Too Little Citizenship," assessing India's mixed progress on the ills Masani diagnosed, from economic stagnation giving way to growth to persistent decay in public life.
A tribute remembers historian Professor Y. D. Phadke, praising his pioneering study of the Samyukta Maharashtra Movement and his eight-volume history of Maharashtra.
